For existing communities

Run your own group on this

A one-page guide for a community that might adopt the Charter and Codes.

If you belong to a club, co-op, union local, neighbourhood association, class or nonprofit, and you want to decide things by one Member, one vote with optional, revocable delegation and a public record, the Charter and Codes are meant to be deployed by any community that chooses them. (Federation Compact, preamble) This page says what you would get, what you would have to settle first, and what does not exist yet.

What you would get
  • Drafts to start from. A Charter and ten codes covering rights, conduct, contribution, treasury, disputes and procedure, published openly. Every default is accounted for as derived or chosen, so you can see which numbers to challenge. (Charter 2.4a)
  • Decision rules. Five classes of proposal with fixed deliberation and voting windows and thresholds, one vote per Member, delegation that expires, and a public record of every vote. (Rules of Procedure 1.3; Charter Article III)
  • A way to settle disputes. Panels of eleven Members drawn at random, a ladder of graduated sanctions, and a community vote that can overturn a panel. (Dispute Procedure Code; Code of Conduct 3)
  • Treasury rules. A public ledger, no purchase of influence, and multi-party custody. (Treasury Code 1, 6, 7)
  • The software. Triarchal Framework is open source under the AGPL-3.0. Any deployment can fork it and run it in full, and a modified version offered to people over a network must publish its source. (Federation Compact 3.1; About The Triarc)
  • The name. A deployment that meets the Federation Compact's minimums may use the name "Triarchal Democracy". "The Triarc" is not available; it is the proper name of the nonprofit. (Federation Compact 4.1)
What you would need to decide first
  1. Who counts as a Member, and how they are verified. The Charter's baseline is anyone aged eighteen or older with a verified account who affirms the charter, and a community may strengthen that by amendment. The Triarc added phone verification. Your group probably has a membership list; decide whether it is the roll. (Charter 1.1; Triarc Membership Code 2.1)
  2. What the votes bind. The documents do not make your existing constitution, bylaws or the law go away, and they do not tell you what a membership vote may lawfully decide in your case. Settle that with your own rules, and with counsel if money is involved.
  3. Whether you want a dividend at all. The minimums the Federation Compact lists do not include one, but the Charter builds one in. Decide early: under the Treasury Code, once the activation gate has opened it never closes. (Federation Compact 2.1) (Treasury Code 5.1, 5.1a)
  4. The founding period. Charter Article IX gives a founder temporary powers that end on measured criteria. Decide who, if anyone, would hold that role in your group, or whether to amend it out. The Triarc Membership Code and Triarc Operations Code apply to the Triarc alone. (Charter Article IX)
  5. Your numbers. Windows, thresholds, the ten-Member participation floor and the sector list are all defaults that a community can change by ordinary proposal. Account for each as derived or chosen, as the Charter asks. The organisational sector list is in the Contribution Code. (Charter 2.4a; Contribution Code 2.3)
  6. Your legal form. If you are incorporated, paying participants while they also elect the directors can collide with the rules on what a nonprofit may distribute to its own members. The Federation Compact describes a two-layer pattern as a recommendation, not a requirement, and says plainly that it is not legal advice. (Federation Compact Article VIII, 8.4)
A short adoption path
  1. Read. The Charter, the Member Bill of Rights, the Rules of Procedure and the minimums in Federation Compact 2.1. They are on the Charter and Documents pages.
  2. Write down what you would change, and account for each default as derived or chosen.
  3. Put it to your own members first, under your existing rules. Our suggestion is to treat the first votes as advisory until your own process says otherwise.
  4. Take advice on the points in the previous section, especially your legal form.
  5. Deploy. Today that means running your own copy of the software. There is no sign-up for new groups.
  6. If you want the name and recognition, ratify the Federation Compact through your own process and publish that in your record. The compact is dormant until more than one deployment has done so. (Federation Compact 7.1)
What the two compacts say

The Federation Compact

  • A party is any deployment that ratifies it through its own process; every party stays sovereign over its own governance, and no council or foundation, the Triarc included, has authority over another party. (Federation Compact 1.1, 1.2)
  • Recognition requires documents that guarantee one member one vote with revocable, renewal-cycled delegation; a public, permanent, append-only record; standing and votes that cannot be bought, inherited or transferred; rights no weaker than the Bill of Rights; disputes settled by randomly selected member panels; and a transparent treasury. (Federation Compact 2.1)
  • A party that falls below the minimums loses the name, not its independence. (Federation Compact 4.2)
  • Disputes between parties go to a panel of eleven drawn from parties not involved, and while fewer than eleven uninvolved parties exist, to direct negotiation on the record. Portability of membership between deployments is permitted and never required. (Federation Compact 5.1, 5.3, 6.1)
  • It says it has no parties yet and activates once more than one deployment has ratified it. (Federation Compact, status note and 7.1)

The Government Adoption Compact

This one is about governments, not clubs. It says the Triarc has no taxing power at any stage, sets out a staged path from an opt-in network through shadow deployments and advisory recognition to a government's formal delegation of authority over a bounded part of its budget, and describes how a sitting official could appear as a default delegate for their own seat. Most of it concerns what a government would have to choose to do. A group that is not a government will rarely need it. (Government Adoption Compact 1.1, 2.1, 3, 4)

Honest limits
What is not true yet

This is software for one deployment today. One public deployment exists, the Triarc, run as an independent instance with its own database. Another group would run its own instance. There is no hosted service, no sign-up for new groups and no support service, and setting one up takes technical skill. (Federation Compact, status note)

Federation is a plan, not a feature. The compact is a draft with no parties. Each deployment runs on its own and the software does not link deployments to one another. Recognition between deployments is, in the compact's words, verified against published documents, with no inspectors. (Federation Compact 2.3)

Everything is a draft. The documents are proposals, not ratified law, and have not been reviewed by a lawyer. The Charter is the Triarc's own constitution and would need adapting for any other group. See Known limits for what the software does not do yet.
